title: CRTP, Mixins and Static Polymorphism
summary: The **Curiously Recurring Template Pattern**: `class Derived : public Base<Derived>`. The base knows the derived type at compile time, so it can call derived functions **without `virtual`**. That is static polymorphism. It suits mixins and interfaces with no run-time overhead. C++23's **deducing `this`** simplifies it.
ideas:
1. Write a CRTP `Shape<D>` with `area()` and `perimeter()`. In a Release build, time 100 million calls against a virtual version.
2. Build the mixins `Printable<D>` (adds `operator<<` using `D::toString()`) and `Counted<D>`, and combine them in one class.
3. Rewrite the first exercise with C++23's deducing `this`.

cards.q: Why can CRTP shapes of different types not be stored in one vector?
cards.a:
Each has a different base, so there is no common base

Static polymorphism gives every class its own base type. For a mixed collection you need virtual functions or a variant.

cards.q: What does CRTP use in place of the vtable?
cards.a:
A `static_cast` to the derived type, known when compiling

The base knows the derived type as its template argument, so `static_cast<Derived&>(*this)` calls it directly and can be inlined.

cards.q: Why does `Counted<T>` give each class its own counter?
cards.a:
Each `Counted<T>` is a distinct class with its own static

Each instantiation of the template is a separate class, so each gets its own copy of the static member.

An explicit object parameter deduced as the real type

`void draw(this const auto& self)` sees the real derived type as `self`, which replaces many CRTP uses.
